stances.claim: Marcos II v. Court of Tax Appeals (June 5, 1997) -- penned by J Torres and concurred in unanimously by JJ Regalado, Romero, Puno, and Mendoza -- became final and executory and stands as a stark indictment of the heirs' 'disregard or even repugnance of the established institutions for governance.'

Ordinarily, a final and executory decision cannot be reopened -- but where facts are shown to be grossly erroneous, or law gravely misapplied, producing a glaring miscarriage of justice, review may be entertained.

Two illustrations show that finality is not absolute: a US rape conviction overturned by uncontroverted DNA/alibi evidence, and the post-EDSA Supreme Court nullification of the Pamaran SBN's acquittal of Ninoy's killers (notwithstanding that acquittals are immediately final and executory).
Jurists are 'not mere legal robots churning out automated results' and do not dispense legalism in a 'sterile vacuum'; they render justice 'to live human beings' and 'give everyone his (or her) due.'

Before any reopening can be entertained, the BIR should first publicly answer factual questions -- how much was collected from levy/auction, how P23B was computed, how it ballooned to P203B, whether crony-returned and ill-gotten assets were included -- and an independent review group co-led by IBP and PICPA, modeled on the Agrava Board, should be formed to examine the factual bases of the Torres ponencia.

notable_anecdotes: Commissioner Lilia Guillermo's viral reply to PBBM -- 'P'wede ba maging role model kayo?' (Can you be a role model?) -- quoted as the column's sociological data point that the public-sector technocracy itself is pushing back on the reopening request.

CJ's own jurisprudential aphorism -- 'jurists are not mere legal robots churning out automated results. They do not dispense legalism in a sterile vacuum without a social milieu' -- one of the densest single-paragraph CJ articulations of the legal-technician-versus-social-engineer ethos in the late columns.

The Agrava-Board parallel deployed not as historical filler but as the operational model for the proposed IBP+PICPA review panel -- letting CJ argue for reopening without naming Marcos heirs as suspects, only as taxpayers whose factual record deserves an independent look.

Specific case anatomy: the four concurring Justices (Regalado, Romero, Puno, Mendoza) named for the Torres ponencia -- making the column read like an internal SC briefing rather than ordinary political commentary.
The 'P23B → P203B' shorthand turned into the column's central numerical motif, with the precise unanswered question 'How did it balloon to P203 billion?' put as the BIR's homework.

one_paragraph_summary: After PBBM, in a Toni Gonzaga interview, asked for the reopening of the estate taxes imposed on his deceased father's properties, the media noted that the Supreme Court judgment requiring the heirs to pay P23B had become final and executory on March 9, 1999 and had since ballooned to P203B with penalties and surcharges. BIR Commissioner Lilia Guillermo's now-viral reply -- 'P'wede ba maging role model kayo?' -- frames the column. Panganiban revisits Marcos II v. Court of Tax Appeals (June 5, 1997), penned by Justice Justo Torres Jr. and concurred in unanimously by JJ Regalado, Romero, Puno, and Mendoza, which faulted the heirs for never questioning the BIR assessments and described their conduct as 'disregard or even repugnance of the established institutions for governance.' May a final and executory decision still be reviewed? Ordinarily no -- but in CJ's humble opinion, when facts are shown to be grossly erroneous, or law gravely misapplied, producing a glaring miscarriage of justice, review may be entertained. He illustrates with a US DNA-evidence rape exoneration and with the post-EDSA Supreme Court nullification of Justice Pamaran's Sandiganbayan acquittal of Ninoy's killers -- proving that even acquittals, normally immediately final and executory, can be undone in extreme cases. 'Jurists are not mere legal robots,' he writes; they render justice 'to live human beings' and 'give everyone his (or her) due.' His procedural recommendation: before any reopening, the BIR must first publicly answer the unanswered factual questions (how much has been collected, how P23B was computed, how it ballooned to P203B, whether ill-gotten assets were included), and an independent review group modeled on the Agrava Board -- co-led by the IBP and the Philippine Institute of Certified Public Accountants -- should examine the factual bases of the Torres ponencia.
